# Brood Benchmarks — the data

Raw output: [`results/report.md`](results/report.md) / [`results/results.json`](results/results.json).
Why Brood lands where it does: [`FRONTIER.md`](FRONTIER.md).

<!-- BEGIN MACHINE (generated by nest run -- docs) -->
Machine: `whklat`, 12-core x86-64, Linux 7.0.0, **2026-09-16** · Brood 0.52.0 (`d0620b3f9`) · Clojure 1.12.5 / JDK 25.0.4 · Elixir 1.21.0-dev (b82c44a) / OTP 28 · Python 3.14.4 · Node v22.21.0 · Ruby 3.3.8 · .NET 10.0.112 · Go 1.24.2. **Brood column re-measured 2026-11-16** (other columns from the field run).
<!-- END MACHINE -->

**Method.** Best of 3 (concurrency rows best of 7, `startup` best of 9 because it is subtracted
from every row), each run `taskset`-pinned (compute on 4 dedicated cores, concurrency on all 12),
after one discarded warmup per language. Every program prints one checksum, and the harness fails
the run if the columns disagree. Deltas under ~5% are drift on this machine; a movement counts
only once a fixed-baseline A/B agrees.

## Compute (wall − startup; the `startup` row is wall)

Columns run fastest to slowest; **bold** is Brood. In `vs best` / `vs avg`, `+` is slower and
`−` faster. The rows are split into tables because not every row compares the same thing.

### Immutable structures vs mutable buffers

Brood, Elixir and Clojure use persistent structures; the rest mutate buffers in place. Brood's
only mutable store is `Table`, which `sieve` uses.

### Concurrency — only two of these are the same thing

Only Brood and Elixir run preemptively scheduled, isolated processes with copying sends. The
other columns are coroutines, threads or tasks on a shared heap: cheaper because they provide less.

- `supervisor` runs only in Brood and Elixir, the two runtimes with a supervisor built in.
- The `pingpong` and `ring` gap is a fixed cost per message: a `receive` loop cannot be
  JIT-compiled, and each message pays a park/wake cycle and a copying send ([FRONTIER](FRONTIER.md)).

## `latency` — what a server actually feels like

Open loop: request *i* is scheduled at `start + i × (1s / 20,000)` whether or not the system
keeps up, so queueing delay lands in the number. Every 20th request occupies ~500 µs of CPU, and
the percentiles cover the other 95%. Offered load is 0.5 of 12 cores, so the tail measures
scheduling, not saturation.

<!-- BEGIN LATENCY (generated by nest run -- docs) -->
| | p50 | **p99** | p99.9 | max | cores | CPU·s | peak RSS | vs best (p99) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** | 7 µs | **54 µs** | 66 µs | 213 µs | 2.0× | 5.46 | 79 MB | −1.3× |
| **Brood** | 14 µs | **70 µs** | 248 µs | 1,776 µs | 1.8× | 4.66 | 187 MB | +1.3× |
| **Go** | 76 µs | **104 µs** | 106 µs | 167 µs | 1.8× | 4.42 | 7 MB | +1.9× |
| **Python** | 3 µs | **423 µs** | 479 µs | 959 µs | 1.0× | 2.52 | 11 MB | +7.8× |
| **Node** | 1 µs | **450 µs** | 643 µs | 850 µs | 1.0× | 2.55 | 58 MB | +8.3× |
| **.NET** | 4 µs | **629 µs** | 12,760 µs | 14,945 µs | 2.3× | 5.98 | 48 MB | +11.6× |
<!-- END LATENCY -->

- The BEAM's reduction-counted preemption stops a long handler from holding a scheduler. Brood's
  p99 is close behind it.
- .NET pairs a low median with the worst tail. Node and Python, single-threaded, wait behind
  exactly one long request.
- This measures runtimes, not frameworks: CPU-bound handlers and no HTTP stack. Each port
  calibrates its own ~500 µs request and must hold the 20,000/s schedule.

## `spawn-live` — 300,000 units held alive, each sent a copied message

300,000 units are held alive at once. Each is woken by a message it must copy, and the replies
are collected one at a time.

### Against the only other runtime with the same guarantees

<!-- BEGIN PEER (generated by nest run -- docs) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** (BEAM process) | 662 ms | 924 MB | 2.2× | 1.87 | −1.4× |
| **Brood** (green process) | 959 ms | 1.30 GB | 3.0× | 2.97 | +1.4× |
<!-- END PEER -->

Brood's weakest row. Most of the cost is the process itself (mailbox, isolated heap, captured
continuation), not messaging; [FRONTIER](FRONTIER.md) has the levers.

### The coroutine runtimes, for context

Promises, `asyncio` tasks and .NET `Task`s share one heap, with no mailbox and no preemption.

<!-- BEGIN COROUTINE (generated by nest run -- docs) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Node** (promise) | 215 ms | 247 MB | 2.2× | 0.52 | −1.2× |
| **.NET** (`Task`) | 261 ms | 138 MB | 1.6× | 0.46 | +1.2× |
| **Go** (goroutine) | 466 ms | 847 MB | 2.2× | 1.05 | +2.2× |
| **Python** (`asyncio` task) | 1.25 s | 361 MB | 1.0× | 1.26 | +5.8× |
<!-- END COROUTINE -->

Isolated primitives elsewhere don't reach this scale. Projected from small runs, Node's
`worker_thread` would need ~3.4 TB at 300k, and Ruby's threads would take over an hour.

## Memory (peak RSS) and startup

Base RSS and startup per language are in the [README](README.md)'s standings table, and startup
is also the `startup` row above. Both are warm figures, with the boot cache populated. A cold
boot cache adds ~19 MB, so compare warm with warm.

## Why C and .NET are faster

C, Go and .NET finish the compute rows several times faster than Brood (see the
[scoreboard](#scoreboard)). Most of the gap comes from choices Brood made on purpose:

- **Static types.** An `int` in C or .NET is 64 bits in a register. A Brood value is a tagged
  24-byte `Value`, and `+` checks the tag first. The JIT removes the check only where it can prove
  the type: integer and float loops, unboxed recursion, indexed vector reads.
- **Code fixed at compile time.** GCC and .NET's tiered JIT inline and vectorise because a
  function cannot change while the program runs. Any Brood global can be redefined (that is hot
  reload), so calls go through a link a `def` can invalidate. Code the JIT doesn't cover runs on
  the bytecode VM, where most of the time is dispatch.
- **Mutation in place.** C overwrites `nbody`'s doubles; Brood builds a fresh vector per body per
  step, because existing data never changes (brood ADR-026). Among the languages with the same
  guarantee, Brood is fastest ([tables](#immutable-structures-vs-mutable-buffers)).
- **Isolation.** A message between Brood processes is a copy. Between C threads or .NET tasks it
  is a pointer.

It isn't one-sided. On `bintree`, C's `malloc`/`free` loses to Elixir's and .NET's collectors,
and on [`latency`](#latency--what-a-server-actually-feels-like) .NET has the worst tail while
Brood's p99 sits with Elixir's and Go's.

**For everyday code:**

- Most programs wait on the network, the disk or a database. There, the `latency` and `startup`
  rows matter more than the compute ratios.
- A ratio multiplies what the compute already costs: 5× a millisecond goes unnoticed, 5× a
  minute does not.
- For dense number crunching (simulations, image and signal processing), use C, Go or .NET, or
  keep Brood for the orchestration and put the kernel in native code: `std/`'s native paths, or a
  WebAssembly component, as the `sqlite` package does.
- Inside Brood, tail-recursive integer or float loops and indexed vector reads compile to native
  code. Rebuilding a large structure on every iteration of a hot loop is the costly pattern.
- What the trade buys: data no other process can change under you, crashes contained to one
  process, and code you can redefine while it runs.

## How to read it

- The [scoreboard](#scoreboard)'s like-for-like row is the aggregate. The field drifts ±10%
  between runs, so read the ordering, not the digits.
- A single sample cannot separate a result from drift; only an A/B can.
- Brood's largest gaps are `nqueens`, `matmul`, `pipeline` (lazy sequences the JIT doesn't cover),
  `json` (an in-language codec) and `bintree` (four non-tail calls per node).

Sources are in [`bench/`](bench/), one file per benchmark per language, so they diff side by
side. Run the suite with `nest run -- harness` (see the [README](README.md#running-it)).
